data.title: Why Netflix Stock Is Down Today and Why There Could Be More “Downside Risk” From Here
data.description:
And down it goes again. Netflix (NASDAQ:NFLX) shares have been hammered over the past year amid a variety of concerns including slowing growth, weaker engagement, tougher competition, unease over its more ambitious M&A strategy and its content pipeline. And now the stock is being subjected to another beating in Friday’s session.

The culprit appears to be the latest note from Wells Fargo analyst Steven Cahall, who has turned from skeptic to bear. Cahall has downgraded his NFLX rating from Equal Weight (i.e., Neutral) to Underweight (Sell) while also lowering his price target from $80 to $57, implying shares will shed 21% over the next year. (To watch Cahall’s track record, click here)

The analyst believes engagement trends are becoming harder to ignore. Netflix averaged about 1.6 hours of viewing per subscriber per day in the first half of 2026, which Cahall estimates is 8% below the comparable period in 2023 after accounting for password-sharing changes and geographic mix. More importantly, he estimates viewing of Netflix’s top 100 original titles declined 3% year over year. Those programs account for roughly 20% of total viewing and, in Cahall’s view, are where much of Netflix’s cultural relevance and member value comes from. He also points to Netflix’s U.S. TV viewing share falling below 8%.

Promotion

55% Off TipRanks

  • Unlock powerful investing tools with TipRanks Premium to make smarter, more confident investment decisions
  • Subscribe to TipRanks Smart Investor Newsletter, and discover new investing opportunities with data-backed stock picks
Learn more about TipRanks Premium

Cahall sees the streaming giant trying to compensate by broadening engagement. The platform is putting more emphasis on gaming, documentaries, reality programming and video podcasts, while its recommendation system appears to be encouraging viewers to explore a wider range of titles. The analyst sees an opportunity to turn Netflix into a broader entertainment hub, but argues that the company cannot afford to lose the blockbuster originals that generate the most attention.

Meanwhile, his analysis of more than 150 major titles leads him to expect a weaker second-half 2026 slate. Cahall estimates viewing of the top 100 Netflix originals will fall 21% year over year, while additional viewing from less prominent titles keeps total hours roughly flat. His base case calls for 96 billion viewing hours, compared with 101 billion in his bull case and 93 billion in his bear case. He also sees higher churn risk heading into 2027.

The analyst sees “tougher choices ahead.” The company could ramp up content spending, although that would take time to produce results, license more third-party programming such as live sports from Fox or NBCUniversal, or pursue acquisitions. Any of these paths could make the Netflix story more complicated.

The analyst also acknowledges several ways his bearish thesis could prove wrong. Netflix is spending record amounts on content and has repeatedly delivered unexpected breakout hits. Its international slate is also difficult to forecast and could provide upside to his viewing estimates. Finally, Cahall notes that Netflix could retain more pricing power and deliver stronger margins than he currently expects.

Nevertheless, despite Netflix’s forward P/E already having already fallen from around 30x to 21x, Cahall sees “more downside risk.”

Cahall, however, is currently the Street’s lone NFLX bear. Elsewhere, the stock claims an additional 25 Buys and 6 Holds, for a Strong Buy consensus view. At $95, the average price target points to 12-month returns of 32%. (See NFLX stock forecast)

data.title: ‘Recognize the Shift,’ Says Investor About SanDisk Stock
data.description:
Sandisk (NASDAQ:SNDK) has been undergoing a significant change in its business. The NAND flash specialist is benefiting from a major surge in demand for storage, driven in large part by the rapid expansion of AI data centers. That demand has been showing up in the company’s results (and the stock’s incredible performance – up by 1,532% over the past year), while the company is also shifting toward higher-value products and longer-term customer agreements that could support stronger margins and more predictable revenue.

The question now is whether investors have fully recognized what the shift could mean for Sandisk’s long-term earnings power.

This is a point brought up by an investor using the moniker Future Stack Investment (FSI). FSI argues that investors are still underestimating the transformation. The investor points to Sandisk’s New Business Model (NBM), which relies on longer-term agreements with customers and could provide a more stable foundation for margins and earnings. Rather than depending as heavily on short-term NAND pricing, these contracts give Sandisk greater visibility into future demand and revenue.

Promotion

SNDK has a long & short ETF? Explore SNXX & SNDQ

FSI also sees the changing revenue mix as important. Data center demand has become a much larger part of the business as AI infrastructure requires more storage. That shift means Sandisk is selling into an area where customers can place greater value on performance, capacity and supply reliability. In the investor’s view, this can raise the economic value of each bit Sandisk sells.

Then there’s the potential for margin expansion. Management has outlined long-term targets of roughly 80% non-GAAP gross margins and 75% operating margins for fiscal 2028 through 2030. Those figures are far removed from the economics of a traditional commodity-memory business and, if achieved, would imply substantially higher normalized earnings.

Nonetheless, all that does not eliminate the risks. Sandisk remains exposed to NAND pricing and semiconductor cyclicality, while expectations for AI-related demand are already high. The stock’s huge run also means investors are paying much closer attention to whether the company can deliver on its ambitious margin and contract targets.

Still, FSI’s central argument is that Sandisk should not be viewed simply as a conventional NAND play. If its contractual model, data center exposure and margin expansion all develop as management expects, the company could have a much higher and more durable earnings base than the market has historically assigned to a memory stock.

“The company is now turning into a differentiated flash business that is gaining exposure to AI and data center demand. I think there’s a nice medium-term opportunity for investors,” FSI summed up. “Sandisk’s shift to higher-value storage products is not getting the attention it deserves. This is creating a more durable earnings stream, and there’s still plenty of room for upside.”

To this end, FSI rates SNDK stock a Strong Buy. (To watch FSI’s track record, click here)

That is also the rating assigned by the analyst consensus, which is based on 14 Buys and 2 Holds. At $2,182.50, the average price target offers 12-month returns of 26%. (See SNDK stock forecast)

data.title: Microsoft vs. Alphabet: One AI Stock Gets an Upgrade, but the Sidelines Call for the Other, Says Top Investor
data.description:
Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) and Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) are reaching an interesting point in their AI spending race. Both companies are committing enormous sums to data centers and computing infrastructure, but investors are getting a different mix of businesses for roughly the same valuation. Microsoft has Azure and its enterprise software ecosystem, while Alphabet still has the huge cash-generating businesses of Search and YouTube supporting its AI push.

The valuation gap between the two has also largely disappeared. Microsoft’s forward P/E is at about 23.3 times expected 2027 earnings, compared with roughly 22.9 times for Alphabet. With only a small difference between the multiples, the comparison becomes much more about the earnings each company can produce over the next few years.

That is the focus of the analysis from an investor using the pseudonym The Alpha Analyst (AA). AA previously had a stronger preference for Microsoft, but argues that Alphabet’s improving growth and profitability have changed the relative setup.

Promotion

55% Off TipRanks

  • Unlock powerful investing tools with TipRanks Premium to make smarter, more confident investment decisions
  • Subscribe to TipRanks Smart Investor Newsletter, and discover new investing opportunities with data-backed stock picks
Learn more about TipRanks Premium

That’s not to say Microsoft no longer has a compelling AI opportunity. Azure is benefiting from demand for AI computing, while Microsoft can also monetize AI through products such as Microsoft 365 Copilot. Its broad enterprise customer base gives the company an established distribution channel for new AI services.

But the company is also spending heavily to build the infrastructure needed to support that demand. AA points to the scale of the company’s capital investment and the pressure this can place on cloud margins. Azure can continue producing strong growth, but AA argues that Microsoft’s cloud gross margins have remained relatively stagnant, making it harder for further revenue growth to translate into the kind of margin expansion investors might expect from such a large AI investment.

Alphabet presents a different combination of growth drivers. Google Cloud is expanding while its operating margins are improving, giving the business scope to contribute both additional revenue and greater profitability. AA expects Alphabet’s revenue growth to exceed Microsoft’s through 2027, which becomes particularly relevant when the two companies are trading at almost the same earnings multiple.

AA also highlights Alphabet’s TPUs (Tensor Processing Units) as a potentially important part of the AI story. The custom chips are designed for AI workloads and can be supplied through Google’s cloud infrastructure. AA believes contracted TPU system sales could provide an additional source of revenue that is not fully reflected in current expectations.

There’s also Alphabet’s advertising business to consider. Search and YouTube continue to generate substantial cash, giving Alphabet the financial capacity to fund its AI investments while those newer businesses develop. The company therefore does not need every part of its AI strategy to deliver immediate returns for the overall business to keep growing.

For AA, the comparison now comes down to the forward earnings setup rather than a simple valuation argument. At roughly 23.3 times expected 2027 earnings for Microsoft and 22.9 times for Alphabet, the two stocks are being priced similarly. The question is how effectively Microsoft can turn its AI infrastructure spending into profitable growth, compared with Alphabet’s combination of advertising, Cloud margin expansion, revenue growth and potential TPU sales.

Bottom line, Alpha Analyst now has a clear preference. “Alphabet is upgraded to Buy as its topline growth, cloud margin trajectory, and underappreciated TPU revenue offer superior forward risk-reward versus Microsoft’s,” the 5-star investor said. “Microsoft is downgraded to Hold; valuation edge has closed, and capex drag plus stagnant cloud gross margins limit near-term upside despite strong monetization trends.” (To watch The Alpha Analyst’s track record, click here)

Wall Street, however, does not see a reason to choose between the pair, with the analyst consensus rating both stocks as Strong Buys. MSFT stock is expected to gain 15% over the next year, given the average price target lands at $571.41. GOOGL’s average price target clocks in at $429.31, a figure factoring in 12-month returns of 24%. (See MSFT stock forecast or GOOGL stock forecast)

data.title: ‘Are You Ready?’ Says Top Investor About Micron Stock
data.description:
Micron (NASDAQ:MU) is heading into its fiscal fourth-quarter results on Sept. 30th with expectations already running extremely high.

Anyone following market trends will know that the stock has had a remarkable run, even when accounting for its recent pullback. To wit, the shares have gained 479% over the past year. That rally reflects a dramatic shift in the company’s earnings profile as AI infrastructure has driven demand for memory and pushed pricing higher.

The bigger question now is whether Micron can turn those extraordinary conditions into something more durable. The company is still benefiting from strong demand and tight supply, but after such a huge move in the shares, the market is looking beyond the next quarterly result and toward how sustainable the current earnings cycle can be.

Promotion

Discover why XOVR identified Kalshi as an attractive private investment opportunity.

Investor Julia Ostian, who ranks among the top 4% of investors on TipRanks, has a bullish view of that longer-term picture, pointing to several developments that she believes could make this memory cycle different from previous ones.

A key part of the argument is Micron’s growing use of long-term customer agreements. Ostian highlights contracts covering around 20% of the company’s DRAM volume and roughly one-third of its NAND volume through 2030. Those agreements come with about $22 billion in financial commitments, giving Micron substantially more visibility into future demand than it typically has during a memory upcycle.

That is important because memory has historically been a highly cyclical business. Prices can rise sharply when supply is tight, only to fall when manufacturers add too much capacity. The 5-star investor sees the new contractual structure as one way Micron can reduce some of that volatility, particularly as AI servers require much larger amounts of high-performance memory.

Ostian also points to Micron’s balance sheet. The company has about $24.43 billion in net cash, providing considerable financial flexibility as it expands production and invests in technologies tied to AI infrastructure.

At the same time, the investor acknowledges how the stock’s momentum cooled after its enormous rally. That makes the upcoming results particularly important. Strong revenue and margin growth may already be reflected to some degree in expectations, so investors will be watching for evidence that demand, pricing and contracted business can remain strong beyond the current peak.

For Ostian, the central issue is therefore not simply whether Micron can deliver another strong quarter. It is whether the AI-driven memory boom, combined with long-term contracts and a strong balance sheet, represents a more durable change in the company’s earnings power.

All told, Ostian rates MU stock a Buy. (To watch Ostian’s track record, click here)

Micron also gets plenty of support on Wall Street. The stock claims a Strong Buy consensus rating, based on a mix of 29 Buys and 1 Hold. At $1,564.44, the average price target offers one-year upside of 60%. (See Micron stock forecast)

data.title: ‘Gamble Away (But Keep Some Chips),’ Says Investor About Rocket Lab Stock
data.description:
Rocket Lab (NASDAQ:RKLB) stock is climbing today as the broader market rebounds following the Federal Reserve’s latest interest-rate decision. The company is also attracting attention after fully financing its planned acquisition of Iridium, including a $1.94 billion share offering and amended debt facilities.

Meanwhile, the company has been widening its remit. Rocket Lab now makes spacecraft and satellite components, launches its own rockets and is preparing to enter a much larger part of the launch market.

Its launch business is built around two rockets. Electron is Rocket Lab’s existing small rocket, designed to put smaller satellites into orbit and already used regularly by commercial and government customers. Neutron is the much larger rocket under development, aimed at bigger satellites and more demanding missions. Neutron has yet to fly, making its development one of the biggest factors behind the stock.

Promotion

55% Off TipRanks

  • Unlock powerful investing tools with TipRanks Premium to make smarter, more confident investment decisions
  • Subscribe to TipRanks Smart Investor Newsletter, and discover new investing opportunities with data-backed stock picks
Learn more about TipRanks Premium

An investor with the moniker Future Stack Investment (FSI) has been assessing the company’s prospects and believes Rocket Lab’s existing business makes that gamble more interesting.

The company’s latest results showed strong growth, with revenue rising sharply as its space systems operation expanded. That business makes spacecraft, satellite components and other hardware, and has become a much larger part of Rocket Lab than its launch operation.

The underlying financial picture also improved, with higher margins and a smaller loss. FSI sees this as important because Rocket Lab is building a business that can generate revenue before Neutron even enters service.

The main issue is cash. Rocket Lab has a substantial backlog of orders, but it is still spending heavily to expand the business and develop Neutron. FSI argues that the company now needs to turn that backlog into stronger profits and cash flow rather than continually relying on fresh capital.

Neutron still represents the big opportunity. A successful medium-lift rocket would allow Rocket Lab to compete for much larger government and commercial contracts. It could also work alongside the company’s spacecraft and satellite businesses, allowing Rocket Lab to provide more of an entire mission rather than simply selling a launch.

Rocket Lab expects to have the first Neutron rocket at the launch pad by the fourth quarter of 2026, although its inaugural flight could be pushed into 2027. Any major delay could put pressure on the stock, particularly because investors are already assigning significant value to what Neutron could become.

At the same time, the planned acquisition of Iridium adds another dimension. Bringing the satellite communications company into Rocket Lab would give it an established business with recurring revenue, while potentially creating more opportunities to combine its launch and spacecraft capabilities with Iridium’s satellite network.

FSI therefore sees Rocket Lab as more than a bet on one new rocket. Electron provides an established launch business, space systems is driving growth, and Iridium could add a substantial recurring-revenue operation. Neutron is the piece that could tie those businesses together and open a much larger market.

Nevertheless, the risks are still considerable. Neutron could be delayed, cash burn could remain high and further share issuance could dilute existing investors. But with a growing business already in place, FSI believes investors should take that risk, although the “size of the position needs to allow the story to develop.”

Bottom line, FSI rates RKLB a “speculative” Buy. (To watch Future Stack Investment’s track record, click here)

Most Street analysts agree. Based on a mix of 14 Buys and 3 Holds, the stock claims a Strong Buy consensus rating. The analysts see one-year upside of 62%, given the average price target clocks in at $110.13. (See RKLB stock forecast)

data.title: ‘It Can Be Done,’ Says Top Investor About Microsoft Stock
data.description:
Like its hyperscaler peers, Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) has a lot riding on artificial intelligence, but the company’s latest numbers suggest that its huge AI spending is starting to translate into real business growth. Rather than relying solely on excitement around new AI products, Microsoft is seeing stronger revenue and profits from the infrastructure supporting those workloads.

That matters because the biggest question around AI spending is whether those investments can generate enough revenue and profit to justify the enormous costs involved. Microsoft’s recent results provide some evidence that the economics are beginning to work.

Top Investor Yiannis Zourmpanos, who ranks among the top 1% of investors on TipRanks, has been taking a close look at that dynamic and argues that Microsoft’s AI story is becoming much more about financial performance than potential.

Promotion

55% Off TipRanks

  • Unlock powerful investing tools with TipRanks Premium to make smarter, more confident investment decisions
  • Subscribe to TipRanks Smart Investor Newsletter, and discover new investing opportunities with data-backed stock picks
Learn more about TipRanks Premium

One of the biggest figures highlighted by Zourmpanos is Microsoft’s new Agents and Infrastructure segment. Under the company’s new segment structure, the recast figures show the business generated $268.1 billion in FY2026 revenue, up 22.6% from $218.8 billion a year earlier. Operating income rose 23.1% to $136.4 billion, lifting the operating margin from roughly 50.7% to 50.9%. That came despite Microsoft increasing capital expenditure by 79.6%.

For the investor, that combination is important. Microsoft is spending heavily to build the infrastructure needed for AI, yet the additional investment has not prevented the business from maintaining strong profitability. Instead, revenue and operating income are growing alongside the spending.

Azure provides another talking point for the bulls. The cloud platform grew 40% during fiscal 2026, and management expects growth of around 45% on a constant-currency basis in the following quarter. That suggests demand for cloud computing and AI workloads remains substantial.

The investor also points to Microsoft’s plans to meaningfully expand its data center footprint. The company currently has roughly 12 GW of capacity and plans to take that figure above 38 GW by 2032. That is a huge infrastructure commitment, but Zourmpanos sees it as evidence of how much capacity Microsoft expects AI workloads to require.

There are risks, however. Microsoft’s relationship with OpenAI creates some concentration risk, while massive infrastructure spending could put pressure on free cash flow. The investor also notes that AI-related capital expenditure across the industry has reached extraordinary levels.

Still, Zourmpanos argues that Microsoft’s valuation gives investors some room for that spending to pay off, as the underlying business continues to produce strong growth and margins. “I think the market is underestimating the fact that Microsoft is demonstrating to everyone that high AI CapEx can still work without killing economics,” the 5-star investor summed up. “Nearly doubling CapEx at 22%+ growth and 51%+ margins is truly something special. Being optimistic, if Azure continues growing at more than 40%, then 25x forward P/E seems to be very reasonable.”

Bottom line, Zourmpanos rates MSFT stock a Buy. (To watch Zourmpanos’ track record, click here)

So do 33 of the Street’s analysts, who, with the addition of 1 Hold, all coalesce to a Strong Buy consensus view. Over the next year, shares are expected to appreciate by 15%, given the average target stands at $571.41. (See MSFT stock forecast)

data.title: ‘Think It Over’ Says Top Investor About Oracle Stock
data.description:
Along with plenty of other tech giants, Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) stock is up in Thursday’s trading, but investors will be hoping that, unlike after its recent earnings report, no reversal will take place.

Recall, the company delivered strong operating metrics in its recent quarterly readout, but that did little for the shares. The stock initially jumped after the company reported its fiscal first-quarter results on Sept. 10, gaining as much as 8.5% during the following session. Those gains quickly faded, however, with the shares ultimately closing almost 2% lower.

That reaction highlights the disconnect between Oracle’s underlying growth and some of the concerns hanging over the stock. The company is spending heavily to build the infrastructure needed to support the AI boom, while taking on substantial debt and relying on major future business commitments. For investors, the question is whether Oracle’s rapid cloud growth can justify those risks.

Promotion

High conviction ORCL bears now have this Tradr ETF

Investor Keith Noonan, who contributes to The Motley Fool and ranks among the top 4% of investors on TipRanks, argues that the recent numbers show why Oracle still deserves attention. Fiscal Q1 revenue climbed almost 30% year over year to $19.4 billion, beating Wall Street’s $19.1 billion consensus estimate. Adjusted earnings came in at $1.92 per share, also ahead of the expected $1.74. Oracle’s cloud operations, particularly demand linked to AI workloads, were a major contributor to the strong performance.

Management also raised its expectations for the full fiscal year. Oracle now expects at least $90 billion in revenue and adjusted earnings of $8.10 per share, compared with its previous forecasts of roughly $90 billion and $8.05, respectively.

Still, Noonan points to several issues that help explain the market’s muted response. Oracle expects to take around $700 million in restructuring costs, partly related to layoffs. Those charges will weigh on near-term results, although the changes could reduce costs over time.

There was also uncertainty surrounding Larry Ellison’s proposed sale of up to 50 million Oracle shares, worth roughly $7.15 billion at the current price. Ellison later withdrew the plan, removing an immediate source of selling pressure. Even if the sale had gone ahead, he would still have retained around 1.1 billion shares.

The investor’s bigger concern is Oracle’s balance sheet. The company finished the quarter with $36.3 billion in cash and roughly $117 billion of debt. That becomes more important given the enormous capital spending required to expand its AI infrastructure.

Much of that investment is tied to Oracle’s massive $300 billion agreement with OpenAI. Noonan notes that the scale of the commitment creates additional risk if OpenAI’s business fails to develop as expected.

Even so, with Oracle down about 26% for the year and 56% from its peak, Noonan sees a valuation that better reflects those concerns. With revenue expected to grow about 34% this year and adjusted earnings around 19%, the investor believes the current valuation leaves room for the company’s AI-driven growth to translate into stronger earnings over time. “While the company has substantial debt and capital expenditures that could create problems if the company’s big deal with OpenAI doesn’t pan out, the stock looks reasonably valued at current prices,” the 5-star investor summed up. “With strong sales growth and the potential for earnings growth to accelerate as spending falls, the shares look like a worthwhile buy.” (To watch Noonan’s track record, click here)

The Street agrees. Based on a mix of 25 Buys vs. 4 Holds, the analyst consensus rates the stock a Strong Buy. At $251.77, the average price target implies shares will gain 67% in the months ahead. (See ORCL stock forecast)

data.title: ‘If AI Infrastructure Was a Miracle,’ Says Investor About CoreWeave Stock
data.description:
CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV) stock is trending lower in Thursday’s session after announcing plans to raise $3 billion through a convertible debt offering. The financing comes as the company continues to pursue a rapid expansion of its business, adding another layer to the debate over how sustainable its growth will be.

CoreWeave has emerged as one of the biggest names in the AI infrastructure market. The company provides the computing power needed to train and run demanding AI models, putting it at the center of the huge spending wave surrounding artificial intelligence. The major tech companies are committing billions of dollars to AI infrastructure, and CoreWeave has been positioned to capture part of that spending.

That opportunity has translated into rapid growth, a huge backlog of contracted business and ambitious expansion plans. CoreWeave generated $2.58 billion in revenue in Q2, up 112% from a year earlier. Its revenue backlog also reached roughly $104 billion at the end of June. But CoreWeave’s model comes with a major catch: supplying all that computing capacity requires enormous upfront investment. The company spent about $9.4 billion on capital expenditures during the quarter, highlighting just how much money is required to support its expansion.

Promotion

Double your CRWV exposure with Tradr's CWVX

That is where investor Andres Veurink takes a dim view of the stock. Veurink argues that investors should look beyond CoreWeave’s headline revenue growth and massive AI backlog and focus on what the company is actually earning from the infrastructure it is building.

The investor’s main concern is that CoreWeave’s impressive adjusted EBITDA margins do not translate into comparable earnings for shareholders. In Q2, the company reported a 59% adjusted EBITDA margin, generating $1.51 billion in adjusted EBITDA. Yet it still recorded a $626 million net loss. Interest expense alone reached $640 million during the quarter, showing how much of the operating profit is being absorbed by the company’s financing costs.

Capital intensity is another major issue. CoreWeave needs to keep spending billions of dollars to expand its computing capacity, meaning strong demand alone is not enough. The economics of that additional capacity have to remain attractive. Veurink points to declining revenue per gigawatt as a warning sign that each new increment of infrastructure may not generate the same level of revenue as earlier capacity.

The investor also sees risks from the rapid pace of GPU development. CoreWeave is spending heavily on hardware that can become economically less attractive as newer generations arrive. If GPU rental rates decline while depreciation and financing costs remain high, the company’s margins could come under pressure.

For Veurink, this makes CoreWeave a much more complicated investment than the headline AI growth story suggests. The company has substantial demand and a roughly $104 billion contracted backlog, but the investor believes its leverage, capital requirements and unit economics create significant risks for shareholders.

Accordingly, Veurink rates the stock a Sell. (To watch Veurink’s track record, click here)

On the Street only one analyst agrees with that assessment, and with an additional 16 Buys and 6 Holds, the stock claims a Moderate Buy consensus rating. The average price target lands at $138.25, a figure pointing to 12-month returns of 73%. (See CRWV stock forecast)

data.title: ‘Before It Wakes Up,’ Says Top Investor About Micron Stock
data.description:
Micron (NASDAQ:MU) has had an extraordinary run, with the stock climbing more than 1,000% since the start of 2025 as investors have piled into the computer memory maker on the back of the AI boom.

But that momentum has cooled somewhat. The stock has retreated by 21% from its June high and has spent the past couple of months largely moving sideways. That creates an interesting setup for investors, as Micron’s underlying fundamentals remain strong even as the stock has lost some of its momentum.

AI servers require far more memory than traditional systems, and the rapid expansion of data center infrastructure is putting additional pressure on suppliers. At the same time, memory manufacturers have been relatively cautious about adding capacity after previous cycles left the industry dealing with oversupply and falling prices. That has helped create a much tighter supply-demand environment, particularly for the memory products needed to support AI workloads.

Promotion

Learn why XOVR invested in Kalshi and the investment thesis behind one of its newest private holdings.

The question now is whether Micron’s fundamentals can provide another catalyst for the shares after such a huge run. Cash Flow Venue (CFV), an investor who ranks among the 3% of investors on TipRanks, believes Micron has just provided one.

CFV points to Micron’s introduction of a new 512GB DDR5 memory module designed for next-generation data center servers. The product offers much higher memory capacity while also targeting improved energy efficiency, an important consideration as AI workloads put greater demands on data center infrastructure. As servers handle larger AI models and datasets, memory capacity and power consumption are becoming more important considerations alongside raw computing performance.

The investor sees the announcement as more than simply another product launch. CFV believes the broader memory supply-demand picture could remain unusually tight for several years, potentially through 2030. That would mark a significant departure from the boom-and-bust cycles that have historically defined the memory industry. If demand continues to outpace new supply, Micron could have more pricing power and greater visibility into its revenue than it typically enjoys during a memory upcycle.

That thesis has HBM right at the heart of it. HBM is one of the main areas where AI demand is putting pressure on memory supplies, as the technology is critical to AI accelerators. But Micron is not relying on HBM alone. Conventional DRAM is also benefiting from stronger server demand, while NAND stands to benefit from the broader expansion of data center storage. Micron has said its 2026 HBM supply is fully committed, giving the company significant visibility into demand.

data.title: 2 ‘Strong Buy’ Stocks Where a Short Squeeze Could Be Brewing
data.description:
Should you short stocks right now? That’s a good question, and it’s one with no clear answer. There’s still a bullish feeling in the air, but volatility is rising, and there’s no guarantee the bulls will keep running. In a market like this, it can be tempting to bet against stocks.

Shorting a stock can be a fast track to profits, but it’s also a fast track to risk. A short seller borrows shares and sells them, hoping to buy them back later at a lower price. If the stock rises instead, the short seller faces losses and eventually has to buy back those shares to close the position. When a heavily shorted stock rises sharply and forces short sellers to cover, that can create a classic short squeeze, with the resulting buying pressure potentially pushing the stock even higher.

For the retail investor, short selling might have little appeal, but watching heavily shorted stocks can point to potential buying opportunities. If a stock that has attracted a lot of short interest starts moving higher, short sellers may be forced to cover their positions, creating additional demand for the shares. For John Q. Public, that can provide an opportunity to take the other side of the trade.

Promotion

Double your WULF exposure with Tradr's WULX

We’ve gone looking for stocks where a short squeeze could be brewing, using the TipRanks database to get the latest data. On our radar today are two stocks with ‘Strong Buy’ consensus ratings, triple-digit upside potential and significant short interest that could fuel a squeeze. Here’s a closer look at them.

Vera Therapeutics, Inc. (VERA)

We’ll start with Vera Therapeutics, a clinical-stage biopharma company that’s working on new treatments for immunological conditions that feature a combination of high, unmet medical needs and a current lack of effective therapeutic agents on the market. Vera is one of many biomedical researchers working in a ‘high, unmet medical needs’ niche; simply put, that’s where the potential rewards lie. Within its field, immunological conditions, Vera is working on new biological molecules as novel drug agents.

The big news for Vera comes from its clinical program, and this highlights a key point about biopharma and short squeezes: a strong clinical trial result can boost the stock, far beyond expectations – but biopharmas have famously long lead times and volatile share prices, making them common targets for short sellers. This week, Vera had just such a strong trial result to report, which may hurt the short sellers.

The trial report comes from the atacicept program, a drug candidate being studied as a treatment for both IgA nephropathy (also called IgAN, or Berger’s disease) and lupus nephritis. The company’s ORIGIN 3 study, a Phase 3 trial of the drug in the treatment of IgA nephropathy has met its prespecified endpoints, including what Vera described as unprecedented – the placebo-adjusted estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and related composite kidney disease progression benefits. The drug’s safety profile was comparable to the placebo, a positive result, and the company now has plans to submit a supplemental biologics license application to the FDA during 4Q26, seeking full approval of the drug.

We should note that atacicept has already received FDA approval for use in treating adults with primary IgA nephropathy (IgAN) who are at risk of rapid disease progression – but that approval was conditional. The new trial results are leading Vera to seek a full and permanent approval of the drug from the regulatory agency.

Based on the existing conditional approval, Vera has already set a commercial launch in motion, and reports strong momentum in that direction. The company states it has seen 350 patient start forms generated in the first ten weeks after approval for atacicept, which is now branded as TRUTAKNA. The company describes early launch metrics as very encouraging.

Prior to these results, VERA shares were the target of short sellers – and as of August 31, nearly 33% of the company’s float has been short sold. That’s a potential set-up for a short squeeze.

Cowen analyst Ritu Baral, who is rated by TipRanks among the top 1% of her peers, has taken note of these positive results, and writes of VERA, “Today’s 2 yr ORIGIN3 dataset further underscores that Trutakna treatment meaningfully improves IgAN disease progression, likely providing effective kidney function stabilization and driving improvements in kidney outcomes. The annualized eGFR slope delta of +5.0 mL/min/year vs PBO is among the most compelling kidney function datasets generated in a Ph3 IgAN trial, numerically superior than +4.5 mL/min/ year PBO-adjusted benefit for Voyxact, a difference that we acknowledge could fall within the variability of the measure. Importantly, Trutakna drove a 2-year annualized eGFR decline of just -0.6 mL/min/year, function similar to the rate of kidney function loss expected in a healthy population, a finding consistent with the long-term stabilization signal previously observed in ORIGIN2. While the competitive commercial positioning between Trutakna and Voyxact remains a marketing debate, we believe this discussion may increasingly shift towards clinical outcomes.”

Baral gives VERA shares a Buy rating and she puts a $78 price target on the stock, implying a one-year upside potential of a hefty 145.5%. (To watch Baral’s track record, click here.)

That’s broadly in line with the consensus here. Vera’s stock has picked up 12 recent analyst reviews, with an 11 to 1 split favoring Buy over Hold for a Strong Buy consensus rating. The shares are priced at $31.77 and the $75.40 average target price indicates room for a gain of 137% by this time next year. (See VERA stock forecast.)

data.title: ‘Skews the Other Way,’ Says Top Investor About Oracle Stock
data.description:
Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) is betting heavily on the AI infrastructure boom, and its latest quarterly results show why.

Revenue hit a record $19.3 billion in fiscal Q1 2027, up 30% year-over-year, with cloud infrastructure driving much of the growth. Oracle also has an enormous backlog of future business, giving investors plenty of reasons to believe the company can keep expanding its cloud operation.

The problem is that Oracle needs to spend heavily to make that growth happen. Capital expenditure is expected to reach $90 billion to $95 billion for the year, while free cash flow remains negative at around $5 billion. At the same time, a large chunk of Oracle’s backlog is tied to a small number of major AI customers, with OpenAI representing a particularly important piece of the story.

Promotion

High conviction ORCL bears now have this Tradr ETF

Looking at the latest results, top investor Julia Ostian’s concern is not whether Oracle has managed to land major AI contracts. It has. The question is what happens if one of its biggest customers changes its plans.

OpenAI is the obvious risk. Oracle’s backlog has climbed to hundreds of billions of dollars, but Ostian points out that a significant portion is connected to OpenAI’s commitments. If OpenAI were to reduce its spending or walk away from some of those commitments, Oracle could be left with a very large infrastructure bill and less revenue than expected to cover it.

The mismatch between Oracle’s obligations and its customers’ commitments is particularly important. Oracle has to spend money upfront to build data centers and secure the necessary capacity. Those facilities and related financing commitments can last for many years. A customer, however, has more flexibility if its own infrastructure requirements change.

That creates a potentially awkward situation for Oracle. The company could end up carrying the cost of infrastructure built for demand that does not materialize at the expected scale.

Ostian, who ranks among the top 4% of investors on TipRanks, also sees Oracle’s balance sheet as part of the problem. The company is taking on substantial debt while free cash flow remains negative, meaning the business is relying heavily on future growth to justify today’s spending. Customer prepayments have helped the cash-flow picture, but they do not eliminate the underlying capital requirements.

The investor therefore sees Oracle’s huge backlog differently from investors who treat it as almost guaranteed future revenue. For the 5-star investor, the size of the backlog matters, but so do its quality, concentration and the amount of capital Oracle needs to spend to turn those commitments into actual cash. That leaves the company with a potentially valuable AI opportunity, but also a sizeable execution risk.

That risk is not one Ostian is currently willing to take. Accordingly, Ostian rates the stock a Hold (i.e., Neutral). (To watch Ostian’s track record, click here)

data.title: ‘Watch the Customer,” Says Top Investor About Sandisk Stock
data.description:
Sandisk (NASDAQ:SNDK) has become one of the more interesting ways to play AI infrastructure’s surge in demand for data storage. The company sits in the NAND flash market, where demand can be highly cyclical and where periods of strong pricing have often encouraged manufacturers to add capacity aggressively. That can eventually leave the industry with too much supply and put pressure on margins.

This time, however, Sandisk is approaching the cycle differently. The company says it can deliver mid-to-high-teens growth in NAND bits without adding wafer capacity, relying instead on technology improvements and higher productivity from its existing manufacturing base. At the same time, some customers are expanding their commitments and buying more NAND than they originally agreed to, suggesting AI-related storage demand may be running ahead of earlier expectations.

An investor using the pseudonym Pythia Research, who ranks among the top 2% of investors on TipRanks, has been bullish on Sandisk for a while and remains so. But rather than focusing mainly on the current NAND pricing environment, Pythia is paying closer attention to what customers are doing and whether Sandisk can maintain its capital discipline as demand grows.

Promotion

High conviction on SNDK? Try Tradr's SNXX or SNDQ

That customer behavior is becoming an important part of the thesis. Several customers have already extended or expanded their NAND agreements, while others are purchasing additional units beyond their existing commitments. For Pythia, this matters because it suggests customers themselves are revising their expectations for how much storage they will need.

There could also be a less obvious benefit. Sandisk is getting more detailed information from customers about future requirements, including technology, capacity and expected usage over monthly, quarterly and annual periods. That gives management better visibility before making long-term manufacturing decisions.

Pythia believes this could help Sandisk avoid one of the biggest problems in the memory industry: responding to strong demand by spending heavily on new capacity, only to end up with excess supply later. Sandisk says its current growth plans can be achieved without additional wafer capacity, while management claims competitors spent about 2.7 times more capital per petabyte during the recent cycle.

That makes capital efficiency a major element of the story. If AI storage demand continues to rise but Sandisk can increase output through technology upgrades rather than a major capacity buildout, it could participate in the growth without repeating the industry’s usual boom-and-bust pattern.

Valuation also remains attractive. SNDK trades at about 7.6 times forward earnings and 5.9 times EBITDA, while fiscal 2027 revenue is expected to reach around $49 billion, up 142%. Fiscal 2028 revenue of roughly $57.8 billion would put the stock at about 4.1 times sales. The 5-star investor believes that leaves room for a re-rating if Sandisk can sustain growth without heavy wafer investment.

“In conclusion,” Pythia said, “I am still bullish about Sandisk, but the next upside would have to come from execution, rather than NAND rerating. Customer expansions, capital-efficient bit growth, and HBF validation are now my key indicators. If Sandisk is able to satisfy rising AI demand without chasing capacity, I believe that it deserves a different valuation.”

Bottom line, Pythia Research maintained a Strong Buy rating on the stock. (To watch Pythia Research’s track record, click here)

data.title: ‘Not the Same,’ Says Investor About Micron Stock Ahead of Earnings
data.description:
Micron’s (NASDAQ:MU) fiscal fourth-quarter results are coming up on Sept. 30, and into the print, investors face a tricky question: has the stock’s recent pullback created another opportunity, or has the market already priced in much of the company’s AI-driven earnings boom?

The shares have cooled off lately after a huge run, but the bigger story is how much Micron’s business has changed as demand for high-bandwidth memory and advanced DRAM has surged.

That leaves the company at an interesting point as earnings loom. Micron is no longer being viewed simply as a highly cyclical memory stock, but expectations are also much higher than they were before AI demand changed the sector. The focus now is on whether that strength can continue. That matters because the stock could still react sharply to any change in expectations after such a strong improvement in Micron’s financial performance.

That is the backdrop for investor Sharon McArd’s bullish take. McArd argues that AI has changed the economics of Micron’s business, with HBM demand, stronger memory pricing and long-term customer agreements giving the company more visibility and potentially a more durable earnings base than in previous memory cycles.

Micron’s third-quarter results provided plenty of evidence for that argument. Revenue reached $41.46 billion, compared with $23.86 billion in the previous quarter and $9.30 billion a year earlier. Even more strikingly, gross margin jumped to 84.9%, versus 39% a year ago, while non-GAAP EPS came in at $25.11, up from $1.91. Adjusted free cash flow reached $18.3 billion. Management then guided for roughly $50 billion of fourth-quarter revenue and a gross margin of around 86%.

The problem is that Wall Street already expects something very close to those numbers. FactSet estimates call for about $50.4 billion in revenue and $30.89 in adjusted EPS. That means simply delivering a solid quarter may not be enough. Investors will likely focus just as much on management’s outlook for fiscal 2027, particularly HBM demand, memory pricing and supply. With the shares having pulled back recently, the reaction could depend heavily on whether management gives investors a reason to look beyond the next quarter and toward another period of strong growth.

For McArd, HBM is at the heart of the longer-term thesis. Micron has secured roughly $22 billion in customer agreements, including take-or-pay arrangements that give customers greater supply certainty while providing Micron with better visibility into future demand. Some agreements also contain pricing structures designed to support margins.

All told, McArd is bullish on Micron heading into Q4 earnings, arguing that the company’s stronger revenue, margins and cash flow point to a fundamentally higher earnings base. While expectations and volatility create risks, the investor believes HBM demand, customer commitments and elevated margins suggest this cycle could prove more durable than a typical memory upturn.

“For me, the Micron thesis is already visible, so the Q4 report needs to confirm the strength, not create the thesis from scratch,” McArd summed up. “AI memory has become one of the most important bottlenecks in data center buildout, and Micron’s finally getting paid like a strategic supplier instead of a commodity afterthought.”

data.title: Houston, There’s a Problem. Investor Weighs In on SpaceX Stock
data.description:
SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) has built something few companies can match. Starlink is turning its satellite network into a global internet business, while its rocket operation has already changed the economics of getting satellites into orbit. At the same time, the company is pushing into AI and developing Starship, which could eventually cut launch costs even further if it proves successful at commercial scale.

The numbers show how quickly the business is expanding. SpaceX generated about $7.8 billion in revenue in Q2, a 92% year-over-year improvement. Starlink accounted for $4.3 billion of that, with around $1.7 billion in operating income, while its subscriber base came in at roughly 12 million. AI-related revenue was another major growth driver, jumping 247% to ~$2.6 billion.

“Those aren’t numbers you see from an ordinary aerospace company,” says investor Lawrence Nga, who contributes to The Motley Fool. “They show that SpaceX is already building multiple large businesses simultaneously. And the opportunity ahead could be much larger across these segments. In short, I think SpaceX is a great company well-positioned for long-term growth.”

Promotion

High conviction on SPCX? Try Tradr's SPCM or SPCG

However, there is a problem, and it is not necessarily the company itself. It is the price investors are being asked to pay for it.

SpaceX, you see, is valued at around $2 trillion. Against annualized revenue of about $31.2 billion based on its latest quarterly figure, that is a huge valuation, particularly while the company remains unprofitable.

The investor’s concern is that buyers at this level are right now paying for a large part of future success. They are counting on continued Starlink growth, a major and profitable AI business, and Starship eventually proving its commercial potential. If those things happen, SpaceX could become an extraordinary company. But that does not automatically mean the stock will deliver strong returns from its current valuation.

The investor would therefore prefer to wait for the relationship between the company’s growth and its valuation to become more attractive. Several things could happen for that to become the case. One possibility is that SpaceX keeps expanding rapidly while its valuation stays relatively flat. Another is that concerns over its enormous spending, which reached $18.4 billion in one quarter, put pressure on the stock. Delays to Starship or a temporary slowdown at Starlink could also create a more attractive entry point without necessarily damaging the long-term business case.

“That’s the kind of opportunity I’m looking for,” Nga added. “Because the best time to buy a great business isn’t necessarily when everyone agrees it’s great — it’s when the market temporarily becomes less certain about how great it can become.”

Bottom line, Nga’s advice is to hold off until the valuation offers a “better entry point.” (To watch Nga’s track record, click here)

data.title: These 2 2026 IPO Stocks Have Been Hammered — But Wall Street Sees a Bottom Forming
data.description:
IPOs get plenty of press, and rightly so. They are the lifeblood of the markets, bringing new opportunities and new capital into the stock ecosystem. But IPOs also bring hard choices and counter-intuitive results, and those deserve a closer look.

To start with, long-term analysis shows that most IPOs will actually underperform compared to their first day on the market. That first day benefits from high valuations and even higher levels of investor enthusiasm – but enthusiasm will wear off, and bring valuations down with it. In addition, most of the early gains from IPOs are scooped by institutional investors, who have an advantage in subscriptions and allocations.

The result, for retail investors, can be serious losses. There’s a true ‘fear of missing out’ in IPOs, but buying in early may not bring the returns that we’re looking for.

Promotion

CBRS has a long & short ETF? Explore CBRX & CBRZ

And this leads to a natural strategy. Don’t ignore IPOs, but don’t necessarily jump in right away. You won’t miss out if you are patient, wait for the hype to fade, and the lock-ups to expire, and natural buying opportunities to emerge organically. Valuation discipline will pay you back, even if you miss the heady times of the initial trading.

Wall Street knows this, and some of the Street’s top analysts are seeing opportunities in IPO stocks that have been hammered lately. These are both shares that went public earlier this year – and they are down sharply since then. The analysts see a bottom forming, however, and that could mean it’s time for investors to jump in. We’ve opened the TipRanks database, and consulted the analysts’ comments, to see just what’s making these new IPO stocks compelling now.

Cerebras Systems, Inc. (CBRS)

The first humbled IPO stock on our radar today is Cerebras Systems, an innovator in fast AI technology. The company is known for building some of the world’s fastest AI tech and infrastructure, and has developed the largest AI chip ever built. This chip, the Cerebras WSE-3 Turbo (WSE-3T), measures 46,225 mm² and contains 4 trillion transistors. It’s capable of giving 250 petaflops of AI compute power, far ahead of any competitor.

In addition, Cerebras has produced the CS-3, an AI-capable supercomputing system with ‘cluster-scale power in a mini-fridge size.’ This advanced system brings fast AI to life, in fields like cryptography, energy, and medicine, and has found applications in agentic AI. The Cerebras CS systems allow users to build and deploy fast, efficient, AI supercomputer units on-site, accomplishing the company’s mission of making AI faster and more accessible.

Right now, one of the biggest pieces of news for Cerebras was its agreement, this past January, to deploy 750 megawatts of wafer-scale systems at the service of OpenAI, a leader in public-facing AI. The deployment will run in stages, through 2028, and the deal is worth billions. In fact, the OpenAI deal is estimated to be worth $20 billion, a massive commitment from OpenAI, and brings both benefits and risks for Cerebras.

On the benefit side, the OpenAI deal makes up by far the bulk of Cerebras’ current work backlog, or ‘remaining performance obligations,’ which now stand at $25.4 billion. While this ensures revenues over the next few years, it also represents a high level of customer concentration, a fact that has engendered some worry on Wall Street.

Those worries have helped to push the stock down from its IPO closing price. CBRS started trading on May 14 this year, and while the company set the price at $185, well above the expected range of $115 to $125, the stock actually started trading at $350, and closed that first day at $311. Cerebras sold 30 million shares, and when the underwriters had used their options, the company realized approximately $6.38 billion in gross proceeds.

But since then, the stock has fallen by 41%. Headwinds on the stock include the overconcentration worries, which we have noted, but also the weight of the high valuation the stock hit in the IPO, and concerns about the overall applicability of Cerebras’ fast AI technology.

Cerebras has also delivered some mixed results. The company reported $180.1 million in Q2 revenue, up 74.3% from a year earlier, but the figure fell short of expectations by $13.4 million. On the bottom line, the company posted a non-GAAP loss of $0.05 per share, beating the estimates by $0.13.

Writing on this stock for Morgan Stanley, 5-star analyst Joseph Moore sees Cerebras in a solid position to deliver strong results, no matter what the controversialists might be thinking. He writes, “Cerebras remains a polarizing story, but we believe fast inference is becoming an increasingly important part of the compute market and that Cerebras has a unique solution in this category. The company has established itself as a leader in this category, demand continues to exceed available supply, and we see multiple avenues for upside – from faster capacity deployment, disaggregated inference, and broader hyperscaler adoption. While execution against the capacity build remains important, we think the opportunity is expanding and find the stock compelling as we see room for material upside given the demand backdrop.”

Moore goes on to quantify his stance with an Overweight (Buy) rating for the stock, unsurprising in view of his bullish comments. He sets a $279 price target here, implying a 12-month gain of 52% for the shares. (To watch Moore’s track record, click here.)

The general consensus on the Street is clearly in agreement with that bullish take. The stock has a Strong Buy consensus rating, supported by 10 unanimously positive recent analyst reviews, and the average target price of $296 suggests that the stock, which is selling for $184.03, will appreciate by 61% over the coming year. Investor Ryan Vanzo, who contributes to The Motley Fool, believes that for those looking for a potential Tesla successor, one of them is a far more likely candidate to give the EV leader a run for its money.

The difference between the way these companies are going about their business is particularly clear when looking at the latest vehicle launches. Lucid’s Gravity SUV is positioned firmly at the luxury end of the market, with a starting price of almost $126,000. Once options, taxes and other costs are included, buyers could easily be looking at more than $150,000.

That may help Lucid build a premium brand, but it does little to solve one of the biggest challenges facing an EV startup: achieving the volume necessary to build a sustainable business.

Rivian’s strategy looks very different. Its R2 SUV starts at roughly $45,000, with more expensive versions reaching around $60,000. That puts the vehicle much closer to the price range of mainstream consumers. Rivian also plans to follow the R2 with the cheaper R3 and R3X, giving it a potential path toward much greater production volumes.

Vanzo argues that this puts Rivian closer to the playbook Tesla used to build its business. Lucid has lower-priced vehicles in development too, but its planned mass-market model has already been pushed back from 2026 to late 2027, raising questions about how quickly it can expand beyond the luxury market.

The same advantage might extend to autonomous driving and robotaxis. Both companies are developing self-driving technology, but Rivian’s much larger market value gives it considerably more financial firepower. Vanzo notes that Rivian could raise an amount greater than Lucid’s entire market cap through only a relatively small amount of shareholder dilution.

There is also evidence that outside companies see value in Rivian’s manufacturing ambitions. Uber has agreed to purchase as many as 50,000 R2 vehicles as it builds out its robotaxi plans. Its separate agreement with Lucid covers 35,000 vehicles.

That does not guarantee Rivian will succeed, and Uber is clearly spreading its bets. Still, Vanzo sees the larger commitment to Rivian as another indication that the company is better positioned to supply vehicles at scale while developing the software needed for autonomous driving.

For investors willing to accept the risks of an unprofitable EV maker, Vanzo therefore sees Rivian as the more compelling choice. “Despite a higher valuation, Rivian shares look more attractive given the company’s larger manufacturing scale, low-cost model launches, and a seemingly more advanced self-driving tech platform,” the investor summed up. (To watch Vanzo’s track record, click here)

The Street, however, does not seem to be enamored with either EV maker, as both claim Hold consensus ratings. RIVN shares are expected to appreciate by 8% over the coming year, considering the average price target clocks in at $17.06. Interestingly, assisted by a highly bullish call, LCID’s $8.71 average target points to 12-month returns of 115%. (See RIVN stock forecast or LCID stock forecast)

data.title: ‘Entering the Crucial Phase,’ Says Investor About Intel Stock
data.description:
Intel’s (NASDAQ:INTC) turnaround efforts have excited investors, but the chip giant is now entering a more demanding phase. The company is making progress on its 14A manufacturing technology, while the rise of agentic AI is creating a powerful new source of demand for CPUs. But the real test now is whether Intel can turn that technical progress and demand into a profitable foundry business.

That matters because Intel’s valuation already reflects a substantial recovery in earnings. The company is still losing roughly $2.5 billion a quarter in its foundry operation, yet it trades at a higher earnings multiple compared to several much more profitable chipmakers.

With this in mind, an investor using the pseudonym Quantryon Capital (QC) believes the next stage of the turnaround needs to deliver more than encouraging manufacturing updates: Intel needs external customers, higher shipments and a credible path to foundry profitability.

One of the most important developments is Intel’s progress on 14A. The company expects to launch its 0.9 process design kit in October, with Intel’s own product teams already designing products around the technology. More importantly, discussions with external customers are moving beyond technology evaluations and toward questions about production capacity. For the investor, that is a meaningful step toward commercialization because it suggests potential customers are considering actual production rather than simply testing Intel’s technology.

Risk production is expected in 2027, followed by high-volume manufacturing in 2028. QC sees this as risk reduction, but not yet as a reason for a major revaluation. The next important proof points would be a named external customer, a significant tape-out or a firm capacity commitment.

The investor is also watching Intel’s estimates for agentic AI. The company believes these workloads could require four to six times more CPU resources than training, potentially expanding the CPU market as AI inference grows. Intel says server demand is already growing at a double-digit rate, while pricing per core has stabilized.

The problem is that Intel now faces supply constraints rather than a lack of demand. Management expects CPU shortages to persist through 2028. But QC argues that scarcity only creates value if Intel can convert it into more shipments, stronger pricing and better margins. Otherwise, constrained supply simply means lost revenue.

Meanwhile, foundry profitability remains the biggest financial test. Intel is targeting breakeven around the end of 2027, although that could slip into 2028 if additional investment is needed to support new customers. The investor is prepared to accept that delay if it reflects genuine demand. A delay caused by weak utilization, poor yields or unattractive manufacturing economics would be much more damaging.

With Intel trading at roughly 68 times forward non-GAAP earnings and around 25 times forward EV/EBITDA, QC believes the valuation leaves limited room for execution failures. “I now need evidence of commercial traction. External customers, CPU scarcity conversion and packaging economics become more important than another manufacturing milestone,” the investor summed up.

To this end, Quantryon Capital rates INTC stock a Hold (i.e., Neutral). (To watch Quantryon Capital’s track record, click here)

That is also the conclusion reached by the analyst consensus, a rating based on 23 Holds, 6 Buys and 2 Sells. That said, the $116.5 average price target implies shares will gain 18.5% in the months ahead. (See Intel stock forecast)
